name: Giocattolo Group B
hook: Australia's own mid-engined supercar began as a small front-wheel-drive Alfa Romeo coupé, and its name is Italian for toy.
story: Picture a car dealer on the Sunshine Coast of Queensland. His name is Paul Halstead. His business is called The Toy Shop. He has seen an Alfa Romeo prototype, the Sprint 6C, with its engine moved behind the seats. Alfa never sold it. So he decides to build his own. He calls in Barry Lock, an engineer who had worked on McLaren racing cars. Their starting point is the humble Alfa Sprint, a little front-drive coupé. Alfa Australia won't sell them bare shells. So they buy whole new cars and strip them. Out goes the front engine. In goes a mid-mounted engine and a ZF five-speed transaxle. The body gets Kevlar panels and fat arches. The first three use Alfa's V6. Then they switch to Holden's five-litre V8, the one from the Walkinshaw Commodore. Cheaper, and stronger. They name it Giocattolo. The toy. About fifteen are built in Caloundra before the money runs out. Halstead later said it was a great car, and a complete financial disaster.
description: The Giocattolo Group B is a mid-engined two-seat coupé built from 1986 to 1989 in Caloundra, Queensland, by Paul Halstead and engineer Barry Lock. Each one started as a new Alfa Romeo Sprint, stripped and rebuilt with Kevlar body panels, a mid-mounted engine and a ZF five-speed transaxle. After three cars with Alfa's V6, the rest used Holden's fuel-injected 5.0-litre V8. About fifteen were made, making it one of the rarest Australian-built cars.
